title: What slander does inside
hookLine: slander darkens the one who speaks it (Sukhmani 13)

lines: YOU FEEL IT IN YOUR JAW.
cards: Ever notice how a complaint grows each time you tell it? The first time, it's a small thing your brother said. By the third retelling it has a beginning, a middle and a villain.
You've rehearsed it so often you can feel it in your jaw. Your brother has long since forgotten. You haven't, because you've been carrying it around and polishing it.
Slander works like that on the inside. It doesn't stay out there, in the story. It moves in.

teach.b: Among the thirteenth ashtpadi's costs, one goes deeper than the rest. Through slandering the holy, the text says, the mind becomes maleen: dirty, stained, like cloth dipped in mud.

It's an inside cost, happening right now in the person speaking. Every time you rehearse someone's faults, you're the one marinating in them. The Guru Granth Sahib shows this from the other side, too.
The poet-saint Kabir, whose hymns sit in the scripture beside the Gurus', says something startling, in paraphrase: let people slander me; slander does me good. Why?
Because, in Kabir's image, the slanderer washes my dirty clothes for me. My faults move off me and onto their tongue.
It's funny and a little unsettling, and it says what Sukhmani says: the dirt ends up with the one who talks. So what goes in its place?
The Sikh answer is in the Ardas, the standing prayer said at the close of Sikh worship, which ends with sarbat da bhalaa: the good of all, the well-being of everyone, with no list of exceptions.
Not my family, my side, the people I like: sarbat, all. People who say Ardas daily are wishing well, every day, to the very people they might be tempted to slander. That's the swap.

teach.h: FILL THE SPACE WITH A BLESSING.
teach.b: Not just stopping the unkind word, which leaves an empty space, but filling it with a blessing.
A stained cloth doesn't get clean by being left alone. It gets clean by being washed.

how: Sikhs end the Ardas, the standing prayer said at the close of daily worship and many gatherings, with a line asking for sarbat da bhalaa, the good of all; Sukhmani's thirteenth ashtpadi names slander's inner stain.

o: sad and heavy, weighed down by grief
sick in body from bad food or water
stained, like cloth dipped in mud

games.q: what slander does inside — tap the pairs.

s: the stain of slander, in Sukhmani, lands on the person being talked about
the mind of the one speaking becomes maleen, stained.
hymns of Kabir sit in the Guru Granth Sahib alongside the Gurus' hymns
the scripture includes poet-saints like Kabir; his slanderer image is there.
the Ardas asks for the good of Sikhs only
it ends with sarbat da bhalaa: the good of all.

games.q: you've stopped yourself from criticizing someone. there's an empty space where the complaint was. what does this lesson put there?
games.why: a blessing. the Ardas asks for sarbat da bhalaa, the good of all; a stained cloth gets clean by washing, not by waiting.

practice: Bring to mind one person you've been criticizing lately, out loud or just in your head, notice the polished story, and set it down.

In its place, wish them one plain good thing: that they sleep well tonight, that their work goes right, that they're less worried than they seem. If you pray, you can hold them inside sarbat da bhalaa, the good of all.

wordCard.voice: Maleen, dirty, stained. It stains the speaker's own mind; and the Ardas puts sarbat da bhalaa, the good of all, in its place.

orig.note: Punjabi: sarbat da bhalaa, the good of all, the closing words of the Ardas.

carryVoice: Your line: bless instead. A blessing washes what slander stains, wishing the good of all. Until tomorrow, then.

sources.ref: Sukhmani Sahib, ashtpadi 13 (Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 279–280)
Kabir, Raag Gauri: the slanderer washes my clothes (Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 339)
